meta.title: Who really said "The Plays of Shakespeare Were Not Written by Shakespeare but by Another Man of the Same Name"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Huxley. The joke was printed anonymously in The Spectator on 14 January 1860, decades before he was born. Huxley used only the Homer version, in 1925.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Plays of Shakespeare Were Not Written by Shakespeare but by Another Man of the Same Name'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous joke from The Spectator, 14 January 1860. Twain, Chesterton, Zangwill and Huxley all used it — none coined it.

answer.label: Not Aldous Huxley — an anonymous joke from 1860
answer.sourceLine: The earliest strong match Quote Investigator has found is an unsigned news item in The Spectator of London, 14 January 1860, which jokes that the plays ‘were not by William Shakespeare, but by another person of the same name’. That is thirty-four years before Huxley was born. Huxley did use the joke — but the Homer version, in his 1925 novel Those Barren Leaves, and like Twain, Chesterton and Zangwill before him he made no claim to have invented it.

source.excerpt: This rivals the new discovery about Shakespeare,—that the well-known plays and poems were not by William Shakespeare, but by another person of the same name!
trail: The earliest strong match Quote Investigator has located is The Spectator of 14 January 1860, in an unsigned item about a supposed new planet. The researcher Stephen Goranson is credited with finding it the full citation chain ↗.

The joke then spreads under a series of borrowed names across the nineteenth century: an unnamed Frenchman (1868), Harper’s Bazar (1870), an Oxford don in the Homer form (1874), a ‘puzzled pupil’ (1883) and Lewis Carroll in Christ Church common room (1885) the chronological citations ↗.

Mark Twain printed the Homer version in The Century Magazine in 1887 — explicitly as a schoolchild’s howler he was reprinting, not as his own line. Quote Investigator believes that is why the joke later attached itself to him Twain’s 1887 article ↗.

Aldous Huxley’s turn comes in Those Barren Leaves (1925), where a character says the author of the Iliad is ‘either Homer or, if not Homer, somebody else of the same name’. Israel Zangwill had already used the Shakespeare form in 1895 and put it in quotation marks, signalling it was common property the 1895 and 1925 citations ↗.
source.excerptNote: The joke arrives already fully formed, as an aside in a report about the possible discovery of a new planet — which is a good sign it was current before it was printed. Quote Investigator says as much: the remark is highly mutable, and it suspects earlier instances exist.

author.name: Aldous Huxley
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Huxley
author.bio: Aldous Huxley did use this joke — which makes him a more defensible candidate than most, and a more misleading one. He used the Homer version, in a novel published in 1925, sixty-five years after the Shakespeare form was already in print. Repeating a joke and inventing one are different acts, and quotation sites almost never mark the difference.

misattribution.heading: Everyone used it; nobody owns it
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with an unusually crowded set of claimants, and the reason is that most of them really did say it — decades after it was already in print, and without ever claiming to have made it up.

items.why: In Those Barren Leaves a character says the Iliad is by ‘Homer or, if not Homer, somebody else of the same name’. The Shakespeare form predates his birth by thirty-four years the 1925 citation ↗.

Twain’s ‘English as She is Taught’ collects classroom howlers; the Homer joke is presented as a pupil’s answer. Quote Investigator believes this is the origin of the later Twain attributions Twain’s article ↗.

items.who: Put it in quotation marks in 1895
items.why: Writing in The Pall Mall Magazine, Zangwill wrote that he did not care whether Shakespeare was written by Shakespeare or ‘by another man of the same name’ — the quotation marks are his the 1895 citation ↗.

items.scope: Lewis Carroll, Charles Lamb, G. K. Chesterton, Benjamin Jowett
items.why: Each is named in a source from 1885 or after — Carroll in a magazine recollection, Lamb in an 1899 novel, Jowett in a 1901 weekly. All postdate the 1860 printing the chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous joke, printed in The Spectator on 14 January 1860 and in circulation ever since — used by Twain, Zangwill, Chesterton and Huxley, coined by none of them the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why it never dies
lead: The joke works by taking authorship scepticism perfectly seriously and following it one step too far: if the man from Stratford did not write the plays, then they were written by someone else called William Shakespeare. It is a logical shrug, and it has been redeployed against Homer, Moses, Theocritus and the Apocrypha.

That flexibility is also why it cannot be pinned to anybody. A joke that can be restated in twenty ways leaves no fixed string to search for, which is precisely the condition in which a saying drifts toward whichever famous wit is nearest.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator dates the Shakespeare form to January 1860 and the Homer form to an Oxford periodical in 1874, and it is careful to say this is a snapshot: the remark’s mutability makes it likely that earlier instances are waiting to be found. An 1840 review in The London Quarterly Review already lays out, quite seriously, the theory of a ‘Homer II’ who wrote so like Homer I that the world confused them — which may be the straight-faced scholarship the joke was written against.

The pattern is worth recognising because it recurs. When four or five famous wits are all credited with the same line, the usual explanation is not that one of them is lying; it is that the line was common property and each of them used it in front of a writer with a notebook.
